title: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behavior.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: while their basic idea of describing behavior in terms of mathematical equations works well in cases like planetary motion where the behavior is fairly simple, it almost inevitably fails whenever the behavior is more complex.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “An Outline of Basic Ideas” (from p. 1), p. 3. Scope: traditional mathematical and evolutionary explanations in the existing sciences

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.23

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Model comparison can probe examples with public data. The near-universal failure claim and the asserted limitation of natural selection are too vague and broad for existing benchmarks to resolve as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Choose a representative benchmark of simple and complex phenomena, define equation, evolutionary, and program model classes, and compare predictive performance at matched description length. A sharply declining performance of the first two classes only on complex targets would support the restricted empirical claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Meaningful statement and complex behavior lack unique metrics.

Programs and equations can encode one another.

A representative benchmark for all existing sciences does not exist.

fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.2
data existence: 0.35
data adequacy: 0.1
analysis feasibility: 0.2
operationalizability: 0.25

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Horizons can check the planetary-motion half directly. The claim that equations almost inevitably fail once behavior is complex, and that program descriptions then succeed in a way equations cannot, needs a survey of models whose inclusion criteria are themselves interpretive. Published successes and failures are scattered across papers, so existing resources test a slogan's easy clause and leave the universal clause open.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Treat published predictive success as the variable: closed-form or numerically solved equations should predict simple systems such as planetary motion within observational error, and should lack stable predictive models for a pre-registered list of complex phenomena. The claim is refuted if equations routinely predict complex behavior to a stated accuracy.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Failure of equations is easily confused with the current state of technique.

What counts as an equation, as opposed to a program or a numerical scheme, is contested.

There is no census of complex phenomena with a uniform success metric.
